name: THE CHARRED SCALLION & SMOKED CHEDDAR SEASONAL SPECIAL

recipe.history: The scallion — Allium fistulosum, also called green onion, spring onion, or bunching onion — is native to central Asia and has been cultivated in China for over two thousand years, making it one of the oldest vegetables in continuous human use. Unlike bulbing onions, which were selected over millennia to form large, papery-skinned underground spheres, the scallion was cultivated specifically for its hollow, cylindrical green stalks and small, underdeveloped white base — a form that emphasizes freshness, brightness, and the raw grassy allium flavor that is the defining character of Chinese and Japanese cooking traditions. In Japan, negi onions are a cornerstone of the cuisine, used raw in noodle soups, grilled over charcoal as yakitori, and incorporated into dipping sauces and marinades. In Chinese cooking, scallions are the aromatics most frequently used to temper hot oil and begin a stir-fry, their sharp edge softening almost instantly in the heat while releasing volatile compounds that perfume the entire dish. Charring scallions — cooking them over very high heat until the exterior blackens and the interior caramelizes and turns sweet — is a technique found across multiple cultures and traditions, from Mexican cuisine's charred cebollitas served alongside grilled meats, to Japanese yakitori negi, to the Welsh practice of cooking whole leeks and spring onions over open fires. The char transforms the scallion's bright, raw sharpness into something smoky, sweet, and deeply savory.
recipe.history2: Scallions entered American cooking early and stayed — they appear in colonial-era American cookbooks as standard kitchen staples, used primarily raw as garnishes for soups and salads, or in quick pickles. But the charred preparation is a more recent arrival in American mainstream cooking, driven in part by the Mexican-American culinary exchange that intensified in the 1980s and 1990s. In Mexican-American backyard grilling traditions — carne asada, carnitas, al pastor cooked over coals — charred cebollitas, whole scallions grilled over high heat until blackened and tender, are served as a matter of course alongside the meat, their sweetness and smoke the ideal accompaniment. American chefs began incorporating this technique into fine dining and then into craft burger culture as part of the broader movement toward charred and smoked flavors in American food. A charred scallion compound butter, spread on a hot toasted bun, delivers smoke, sweetness, fat, and allium complexity in a single application. Smoked cheddar — a natural pair — adds a low, steady smokiness that threads through every bite, grounding the brightness of the scallion in something more substantial.
recipe.history3_personal: I made charred scallion butter for the first time on accident, or nearly so. I was grilling something — I don't remember what, possibly steaks, possibly nothing more interesting than sausages — and I had a bunch of scallions sitting on the counter that I had intended to use raw. Without thinking too hard about it, I threw the whole bunch directly onto the grates and walked away. When I came back they were charred black on the outside, completely collapsed, smoking and fragrant in a way that was entirely different from anything I expected. I let them cool enough to handle and stripped away the blackened outer layers, and what was inside was sweet and smoky and soft as butter. I chopped them fine and mixed them into soft unsalted butter with a little garlic and flaky salt, and spread it on everything I could reach. The combination with smoked cheddar came later, at a dinner where I had both on the table and someone piled them together on a cracker almost without thinking, and the combination was so obviously right that it felt like a discovery and an inevitability at the same time. This burger was born from that moment.
recipe.history4_philosophy: A seasonal special burger demands a certain quality of intention — it is not the burger on the permanent menu that has been refined and re-refined over years of service, but a one-time or limited argument for a particular combination of flavors that is right for this moment, this season, this week. The charred scallion and smoked cheddar burger is a spring-into-summer burger: it belongs to the season when scallions are at their most abundant and tender, when the grill is being fired up again after winter, when there is still a slight chill in the air that makes smoked, warm flavors welcome. And like all burgers worth ordering, it depends entirely on the patty being cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — because the pickled jalapeño that cuts through the richness of the smoked cheddar and the charred scallion butter requires a fatty, juicy, yielding patty to balance its acidity and heat. A dry patty has nothing for the jalapeño's acid to cut through; a medium rare patty has everything. The whole burger is a negotiation between smoke, fat, heat, and acid, and it only works when the patty is right.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
3 bunches fresh scallions (about 18 scallions), roots trimmed
113g unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
2 cloves garlic, minced to a paste
4 fresh jalapeños, thinly sliced into rounds
1 tsp chipotle in adobo, finely minced
instructions: 1. Make the pickled jalapeños (at least 1 hour ahead): In a small saucepan, combine vinegar, water, sugar, salt, and garlic. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring until sugar and salt dissolve. Pack jalapeño slices into a jar and pour hot brine over them. Let cool to room temperature, then cover and refrigerate. Ready in 1 hour; better after overnight.

2. Char the scallions: Heat a grill or grill pan over very high heat until smoking. Lay whole scallions directly on the grates. Grill without moving for 2–3 minutes until heavily charred and blackened on the first side. Turn and char the other side, 1–2 more minutes. The scallions should be mostly blackened on the outside and completely softened. Transfer to a cutting board and cool for 10 minutes.

3. Make the charred scallion butter: Once scallions are cool enough to handle, strip away the most severely charred outer layers, leaving the charred but still intact inner flesh and some of the blackened exterior for flavor and color. Finely mince the charred scallions — you want about 100g of minced charred scallion. Beat softened butter until smooth and fluffy. Fold in minced charred scallion, garlic paste, flaky salt, black pepper, and lemon zest until evenly combined. Taste and adjust seasoning. Roll into a log in plastic wrap and refrigerate until firm, at least 30 minutes.
4. Make the smoked aioli: Combine mayonnaise, smoked paprika, chipotle in adobo, grated garlic, and apple cider vinegar. Whisk until smooth. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the buns: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer with the dough hook. Add warm milk, water, and egg. Mix on low 2 minutes, then medium 4 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time. Once incorporated, mix on medium-high 6–8 minutes until smooth and elastic. Rise in a covered, oiled bowl for 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

6. Divide bun dough into 4 portions, shape into tight balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, flatten gently. Proof covered 45–60 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F / 190°C for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

7. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 225g each). Form into round patties 3/4 inch thick and 4 inches wide. Press a dimple into the center of each. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.
8. Cook the patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat for 3 minutes until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the skillet. Cook undisturbed for 3 minutes.

9. Flip once. Place a thick slice of smoked cheddar on each patty. Cook 2–3 more minutes, covering the pan in the last minute to melt the cheese. Check internal temperature — target 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest on a wire rack for 3–4 minutes.

10. Toast the buns: Slice buns and spread a generous round of charred scallion butter on each cut side of both the top and bottom buns. Place cut-side down in a skillet over medium heat. Toast 1–2 minutes until golden and the butter has melted in.

11. Assemble: Spread smoked aioli on the top bun. Add shredded romaine to the bottom bun over the toasted scallion butter. Place the rested smoked-cheddar-topped patty on the lettuce. Add a few slices of red onion and a generous pile of pickled jalapeños over the patty. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
